rules.message: SQL embeds 2+ conditional-logic constructs (CASE WHEN branches / IF·IIF calls) — filtering/aggregation in SQL is fine, but conditional business rules here are hard to test and easy to duplicate. Consider whether the policy belongs in app code instead.

A `.reduce(...)` call appears in the same function as a `findMany(`/raw `prepare(` call — a CO-OCCURRENCE heuristic on two independent patterns, NOT proof the reduce consumes that query's result: nothing links them, so a `.reduce(...)` over an unrelated array in a function that queries elsewhere fires just the same, and the finding anchors on the first `.reduce(...)`. The `fetch-many` arm is `\.findMany\s*\(|\bprepare\s*\(` — a bare `prepare(` call, with no `.all()` required. When they ARE connected: if the row set is large, a SQL aggregate (SUM/COUNT/GROUP BY) avoids transferring it; if small and reused, app-side is fine. Decide by data volume.

A `.filter(...)` call and a `.length` access both appear in the same function as a `findMany(`/raw `prepare(` call — a CO-OCCURRENCE heuristic on THREE independent patterns, NOT proof they form one `findMany().filter(...).length` chain: the three may match three unrelated lines, `.length` matches ANY `.length` access (a string's included), and the finding anchors on the first `.length`. The `fetch-many` arm is `\.findMany\s*\(|\bprepare\s*\(` — a bare `prepare(` call, with no `.all()` required. When they ARE connected: if the row set is large, a SQL aggregate (SUM/COUNT/GROUP BY) avoids transferring it; if small and reused, app-side is fine. Decide by data volume.

`SELECT * FROM` inside a string literal — over-fetching every column couples the caller to the table's exact shape (a later `ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN` silently changes what this query returns) and pulls columns nobody reads across the wire. LANGUAGE SCOPE is the set `sql/delete-no-where` states, for the same reason — an opening quote and then the SQL keywords, with no host-language syntax in the pattern — so `.ts`/`.tsx`/`.js`/`.mjs`/`.cjs`, `.py`, `.java`, `.cs`, `.go` and `.rs` are all admitted, C#'s verbatim `@"..."` and Go's backtick raw string included. The MULTI-LINE residual is larger here than for the destructive siblings, because a long SELECT is exactly the statement people break across lines: a Java text block, a Python triple-quoted string, a Go raw-string block or a multi-line C# `@"..."` whose `SELECT *` sits on its own line carries no quote there, and a line-scan cannot see it. In `.py` the two comment axes part company: the SKIP axis reads `//` alone outside `.sql` and config files, so a `#`-commented-out query is read as live code, while the MARKER axis does admit `#` — which is why the suppression offered below is writable in Python. CO-FIRING with `security/sql-string-concat` is intended, not a duplicate: on a Java line like `"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + name + "'"` that rule reports the INJECTION shape and this one reports the OVER-FETCH, two independent defects with two different repairs (bind the parameter; name the columns) — the same ruling `security/weak-crypto` and `security/weak-password-hash` carry on one credential line. Neither rule's silence would imply the other's. List the columns you actually use instead, or suppress a vetted case with `// zzop-select-star-ok`, or `# zzop-select-star-ok` in a `.py` file (the `# // …` sandwich this message used to prescribe is no longer needed — `#` is a marker leader in Python now).

A `LIKE` pattern with a leading `%` wildcard (e.g. `LIKE '%term'`) can't use a standard B-tree index prefix — the engine falls back to a full table/index scan on every call. LANGUAGE SCOPE is the widest of this pack, because the anchor is entirely INSIDE the SQL: `LIKE` followed by a SQL string quote and a `%`, with not one character of host-language syntax in it. Admitted in `.ts`/`.tsx`/`.js`/`.mjs`/`.cjs`, `.py`, `.java`, `.cs`, `.go` and `.rs`. That very portability is what makes one exclusion necessary, and it is the only language-shaped thing here: in the printf family a `%` immediately followed by a conversion letter and then the closing quote is a PLACEHOLDER, not a wildcard — `fmt.Sprintf("... LIKE '%s'", term)` in Go, `String.format` in Java, `"... LIKE '%s'" % term` and the named `'%(term)s'` form in Python all substitute the whole pattern at runtime, so claiming a leading wildcard there would be a claim about text this rule never sees. Those lines are excluded. The exclusion is deliberately narrow — it requires the quote to close IMMEDIATELY after the conversion letter, so `LIKE '%sale%'` (a real leading wildcard that happens to start `%s`) still fires, and `LIKE '%' + @term` / `LIKE '%%%s%%'` still fire because the `%` there is genuinely a wildcard. Its disclosed cost is the one-character search `LIKE '%s'` meaning "ends with s", which is now silent. Python's bare `LIKE %s` (psycopg's unquoted bound parameter) never matched in the first place: the pattern requires a quote between `LIKE` and the `%`. In `.py` the two comment axes part company: the SKIP axis reads `//` alone outside `.sql` and config files, so a `#`-commented-out query is read as live code, while the MARKER axis does admit `#` — which is why the suppression offered below is writable in Python. If this needs to stay a substring/suffix search, reach for full-text search or a reversed-column index; a trailing-only wildcard (`LIKE 'term%'`) stays index-friendly. Suppress a vetted case (small table, offline query) with `// zzop-like-leading-wildcard-ok`, or `# zzop-like-leading-wildcard-ok` in a `.py` file.
